Granville Sharp
gran'vil shärp
n. (Granville Sharp, 1735–1813, English abolitionist and Greek grammarian, first chairman of the Society for Effecting the Abolition of the Slave Trade)
English surname Sharp, from the adjective, keen; Granville, from a Norman place name.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Granville Sharp was a linen-draper's apprentice turned clerk in the Ordnance Office who taught himself Greek, Hebrew, and law, and used all three. In 1765 he found a beaten slave, Jonathan Strong, on a London street, had him treated, and when the owner seized him again fought the case; he then spent seven years on the law until in 1772 the Somerset case established that a slave could not be forcibly carried out of England. He was the first chairman of the Society for Effecting the Abolition of the Slave Trade in 1787 and a founder of the Sierra Leone settlement and of the British and Foreign Bible Society. His Remarks on the Uses of the Definitive Article in the Greek Text of the New Testament (1798) established the grammatical rule that bears his name, by which Tit 2:13 and 2Pe 1:1 name Jesus Christ as “the great God and our Saviour” (Tit 2:13).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines the article as a part of speech used before nouns to limit their signification, and habeas corpus as a writ for delivering a person from false imprisonment.

expand to see more

AR'TICLE, n. In grammar, a part of speech used before nouns to limit or define their application; as the English a, an, the.

HA'BEAS COR'PUS. A writ for delivering a person from false imprisonment, or for removing a person from one court to another.

EMANCIPA'TION, n. The act of setting free from servitude or slavery; deliverance from bondage.

Key Scripture

Tit 2:13 — "Looking for that blessed hope, and the glorious appearing of the great God and our Saviour Jesus Christ;"

2Pe 1:1 — "Simon Peter, a servant and an apostle of Jesus Christ, to them that have obtained like precious faith with us through the righteousness of God and our Saviour Jesus Christ:"

Act 17:26 — "And hath made of one blood all nations of men for to dwell on all the face of the earth, and hath determined the times before appointed, and the bounds of their habitation;"

Exo 21:16 — "And he that stealeth a man, and selleth him, or if he be found in his hand, he shall surely be put to death."

Modern Corruption

The man who freed slaves in English courts also proved from the Greek article that Christ is called God.

expand to see more

Sharp's rule is a real contribution and the dictionary states it precisely: where two singular personal nouns of the same case are joined by kai and the article stands before the first only, both describe one person. Applied to Tit 2:13 and 2Pe 1:1 the construction yields the plain sense that “the great God and our Saviour Jesus Christ” (Tit 2:13) is one subject, not two, so that the texts are direct assertions of the Saviour's deity. The rule was attacked at the time by Unitarian writers for exactly that reason and has stood.

The two halves of his life come from one doctrine. Act 17:26 teaches that God “hath made of one blood all nations of men” (Act 17:26), and Exo 21:16 sentences the manstealer; a man who believes those texts and reads Greek will end up in both the courtroom and the grammar. This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of Sharp himself, though the rule is sometimes dismissed as a piece of apologetic convenience. It was published by a man with no academic post who had already spent twenty years losing money on lawsuits for other people's freedom, which is not the profile of a special pleader.

Usage

"“the great God and our Saviour Jesus Christ” (Tit 2:13) — one subject, by his rule."

"“the righteousness of God and our Saviour Jesus Christ” (2Pe 1:1) — the same construction."

"“hath made of one blood all nations of men” (Act 17:26) — why he went to court."
